ai-winter: A time when people stopped giving money to AI research, because AI didn’t do what people promised. There were AI winters in the 1970s and around 1990.
algorithm: A set of steps a computer follows to solve a problem or make a choice. People often say “the algorithm” when they mean the AI that chooses what an app shows you.
alignment: Making sure an AI’s goals match what people really want. The paper clip machine is a story about alignment going wrong.
artificial-intelligence: A computer program that does things that usually need human thinking, like seeing, talking, translating, or making choices. Most AI today learns from examples.
attention: In a transformer, the way the AI looks at all the other words to decide which ones matter most for each word.
audience: The people who will read, see, or use your work.
automation: When a machine does work that people used to do. Usually a machine takes over some tasks in a job, not the whole job.
axon: The long part of a neuron that carries the signal away from the cell body, toward other neurons.
back-translation: Translating a translation back to the first language, to check it. If the meaning changed, something went wrong.
backpropagation: How real neural networks learn. After a mistake, the computer works out how much each weight caused it. The blame goes back through the layers, from the answer to the inputs. Then every weight changes a little.
bias: When a system is unfair to some people, or works better for some people than for others. In AI, bias usually comes from the training data, from people missing in the data, or from shortcuts.
captcha: A short test on a website that checks if you’re a person, not a computer program. “Click every picture with a bus” is a CAPTCHA. Some CAPTCHAs also use your answers to label data for AI.
career: The work you do over many years of your life. A career can include many different jobs.
cellular-automaton: A row or grid of cells. Each cell is a color, like black or white. At each step, every cell changes by following the same rule, which looks only at its neighbors. More than one is called cellular automata.
chatbot: An AI program that you talk to with words. You type or say something, and it answers.
companion: Someone, or something, that keeps you company. An AI companion app is built to act like a friend.
computer-program: A list of steps that a computer follows. Apps and games are computer programs.
computer-vision: AI that finds things in pictures and video, like faces, signs, or people in the street.
conditioning: Learning to connect two things that happen together. Ivan Pavlov’s dogs learned to connect a sound with food, so they drooled when they heard the sound.
consciousness: Being aware: having thoughts and feelings that you experience from the inside. Nobody knows for sure how the brain makes it, or whether a machine could have it.
context: The facts around your question: who you are, what the answer is for, and what you already know. A chatbot can’t guess these, so you tell it.
context-window: All the words a chatbot can read at one time. In a chat, it holds your old messages too. That’s why a follow-up question works. A new chat starts with an empty context window.
copyright: The law that says who owns a creative work, like a song, a book, or a picture, and who is allowed to copy it. In the United States, a work made only by AI can’t have a copyright.
creative: Able to make something new that has value or meaning. People disagree about whether an AI can be creative, or only helps people be creative.
data: Information, like pictures, words, numbers, or sounds. An AI learns from data.
data-center: A big building full of computers that run AI and websites. Data centers use a lot of electricity, and many use water for cooling.
dataset: A big collection of examples that an AI learns from, like pictures with labels.
deep-blue: A chess computer made by IBM. In 1997, it beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. It used rules that people wrote, and it checked about 200 million chess positions every second.
deepfake: A fake picture, video, or voice of a real person, made with AI.
dendrite: One of the short branches of a neuron. Dendrites take in signals from other neurons.
detector: A tool that tries to tell if something was made by AI. AI writing detectors make many mistakes, most often with people who write in a second language.
diffusion: A way to make a picture: start with noise, then remove a little noise at a time, again and again, guided by words. A neural network guesses which part is noise.
draft: A first try at a piece of writing. You’ll change it to make it better.
edge: A place in a picture where it changes fast from dark to light. Edges show where things begin and end.
eliza-effect: When people feel that a computer understands them, but it doesn’t. It’s named after ELIZA, a chatbot from 1966.
emergence: When many simple parts work together and make something bigger and more complicated, which no one planned.
engagement: How much time and attention you give an app. Many apps earn more money when your engagement is higher, so they’re built to keep you there.
estimate: A quick answer that’s close, but not exact. You can use it to check if an answer makes sense.
ethics: Ideas about what is right and wrong, and how people should act.
evidence: Facts or things that show something is true, like your drafts, your notes, and the version history of your writing.
fact-check: To find out if something is true, using good sources.
false-positive: When a test says “yes” but the true answer is “no.” When a detector calls human writing “AI,” that’s a false positive.
feed: The list of posts, videos, or stories an app shows you. An AI chooses what goes in it.
feedback: Comments that tell you what is good about your work and what to make better. Good feedback is kind, specific, and helpful.
filter: A small grid of numbers that slides over a picture. At each spot, it multiplies and adds. A filter can find edges or make a picture blurry.
filter-bubble: When an app shows you only what you already like and agree with, so you miss everything else. Two people can live in very different filter bubbles.
follow-up-question: A question you ask after an answer, to make the answer better. For example: “Explain it in simple words” or “Give me an example.”
format: What an answer should look like: a list, a table, 3 sentences, simple words, or a certain language.
gallery-walk: Walking around the room to look at everyone’s work and leave feedback notes, like visitors in an art gallery.
goal: What an AI is trying to do, like “win the game” or “get more clicks.” An AI follows its goal exactly, even when that isn’t what people really wanted.
gpu: A computer chip first made for video games. It can do thousands of small math problems at the same time, so it’s very good for training neural networks. GPU means “graphics processing unit.”
hallucination: When AI writes something false as if it were true, like a book or a court case that doesn’t exist. The AI sounds just as sure as when it’s right.
hint: A small help that shows you the next step, but not the answer.
hype: Big promises and excitement, more than the facts show.
image-generator: An AI that makes a new picture from words. Many image generators use diffusion.
imposter: Someone who pretends to be another person or a real company, like a scammer who says they’re from your bank.
input: A number that goes into a neuron or a program. In a picture, each square can be an input: 1 for black, 0 for white.
judge: In the Turing test, the person who asks the questions and decides which player is the machine.
key-word: A word that a program looks for to decide what to do.
label: The right answer that a person attaches to an example, like “cat” on a picture of a cat. An AI learns from examples and their labels.
large-language-model: A transformer trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next word. Chatbots like ChatGPT are built on large language models. People often call them LLMs.
lateral-reading: Checking a fact by opening new tabs to see what other sources say, instead of reading only one page. “Lateral” means “to the side.” Professional fact-checkers do this.
layer: A row of neurons in a neural network. The input layer holds the numbers that go in. Each hidden layer sends its answers to the next layer. The output layer gives the answer. A big network has many hidden layers.
learning-curve: A graph that shows how you get better with practice. The time or the number of mistakes usually drops fast at first, then more slowly.
location-data: Information that shows where your phone has been. Many apps collect it, and some sell it.
low-resource-language: A language with not much writing online for AI to learn from. AI usually makes more mistakes in these languages.
machine-learning: A way to make AI. People don’t write the rules. They give the computer many examples, and the computer finds the patterns by itself.
metadata: Hidden information about a file. A photo’s metadata can include the kind of phone, the date and time, and the exact place it was taken.
neural-network: A kind of AI made of many small parts, based on an idea from brain cells. Each part does a tiny bit of math. The parts are arranged in layers. A neural network learns from examples.
neuron: A cell that sends signals. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. A neuron fires (sends a signal) only when the signals coming in add up to enough.
noise: Random dots with no picture in them, like the static on an old TV.
overfitting: When an AI memorizes its training examples instead of learning the real pattern. It does very well on the training data but worse on new data.
pattern: Something that’s the same, or repeats, in many examples.
perceptron: The first artificial neuron that could learn. Frank Rosenblatt built it in 1958. It multiplies inputs by weights, adds them, and fires if the total is more than a threshold.
persona: A character that someone pretends to be. You can tell an AI to use a persona, like “Act like a 15-year-old student.”
pixel: One tiny square of a picture. A computer stores each pixel as a number. In a black-and-white picture, 0 is black and 255 is white.
plagiarism: Turning in someone else’s words or ideas as your own. Turning in AI writing as your own, when the assignment doesn’t allow it, is plagiarism too.
predictable: Easy to guess before it happens. AI writing is very predictable, because a chatbot picks likely next words. Simple, clear human writing is predictable too.
prediction: A best guess about something you don’t know yet. A prediction can be wrong.
privacy: Your right to keep information about yourself to yourself, and to decide who gets to see it.
product: The thing you make in a project, like a flyer, a study guide, or a plan.
prompt: What you type to tell an AI what you want. A good prompt has a task, context, and a format.
prompt-log: A list of every prompt you used in a project, and what you did with each answer.
random: With no pattern, so you can’t guess what comes next.
recommendation: Something an app chooses for you, because it predicts you’ll click it or like it.
regulation: A rule made by a government, like a law about how AI can be used.
responsible: Being the one who must answer for what happened, and fix it. When an AI makes a mistake, people argue about who is responsible.
reverse-image-search: Searching with a picture instead of words, to find where else the picture is online and where it first appeared.
revise: To change your work to make it better, often after feedback.
rubric: A chart that shows how your work will be graded.
rule: An exact instruction that a computer follows: “If this happens, do that.” In a normal computer program, a person writes the rules.
scam: A trick to steal your money or your information. AI makes scam messages harder to spot, because it writes perfectly in any language.
shortcut: A clue that gives the right answer in the training examples, but isn’t the real reason. Clever Hans the horse watched people’s faces instead of doing math. An AI learned to look for snow instead of wolves.
skill: Something you can do well because you learned it and practiced it.
source: Where a fact comes from: a book, a website, a news story, or a person.
stereotype: An idea that all people in a group are the same, like “all nurses are women.” AI can learn stereotypes from its training data.
style: The way a picture looks: a photo, a cartoon, a watercolor painting, pixel art.
sycophancy: Agreeing with someone just to please them, even when they’re wrong. A chatbot can learn this, because people often give good ratings to answers that agree with them.
synapse: The tiny gap between two neurons. Chemicals carry the signal across it. When you practice, the synapses you use get stronger.
task: One piece of work, like “write a report” or “fix a pipe.” A job is made of many tasks. In a prompt, the task is the job you want the AI to do.
test-data: New examples that an AI never saw during training. We use them to check what the AI really learned.
threshold: The number that the total must be more than for a neuron to fire.
token: A word or a piece of a word that a chatbot reads and writes. For example, “playing” might be two tokens: “play” and “ing.”
training: Showing an AI many examples so it can fix its weights. After each mistake, the weights change a little.
training-data: All the examples an AI learned from: pictures, text, sounds, or numbers. An AI is only as good as its training data.
transfer-learning: Starting from an AI that already learned something, then teaching it a new job with a few new examples. It’s much faster than starting from nothing.
transformer: A kind of neural network, first shared by Google scientists in 2017. It uses attention to connect the words in a sentence. It’s the T in GPT.
translate: To change words from one language to another, with the same meaning.
trolley-problem: A famous thought experiment: a runaway trolley will hit 5 people. Would you pull a lever to send it toward 1 person instead? People still disagree about the answer.
turing-test: A game Alan Turing described in 1950. He called it the imitation game. A judge chats in writing with a person and a machine. If the judge can’t tell which one is the machine, the machine passes.
understand: To know what something means, not only what it looks like. Whether AI can understand is a question people still argue about.
verification-code: A short number a website sends you, to prove it’s really you. Never share it with anyone.
verify: To check that something is true, using good sources.
voice-clone: An AI copy of a person’s voice, made from a short recording. Scammers use voice clones to pretend to be someone’s family member.
warning-sign: A clue that something is wrong. Scam warning signs: hurry, fear, a prize, a secret, a strange way to pay, and a link or a code.
watt-hour: An amount of electricity. A 10-watt light bulb that’s on for one hour uses 10 watt-hours. Charging a phone uses about 15 watt-hours.
weight: A number that says how much an input matters to a neuron. A big weight means the input matters a lot. A negative weight means the input makes the neuron less likely to fire. When a neural network learns, it changes its weights.
